slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: We can't define every word, because definitions would go in circles. So geometry starts with a few undefined terms (point, line, plane) and postulates, which are rules we agree to assume about them. Everything else is defined or proved.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: We can't define every word, because definitions would go in circles. So geometry starts with a few undefined terms (point, line, plane) and postulates, which are rules we agree to assume about them. Everything else is defined or proved.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• undefined term A basic word we describe but do not define, like point, line and plane.
  • definition An exact meaning built from words we already have.
  • postulate (axiom) A starting rule we accept without proof.
  • theorem A statement that has been proved from definitions, postulates and earlier theorems.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
What does 'undefined' mean for a point?

Read the worked steps
StepReason
We don't define 'point' with other words.It is one of our starting words.
Instead we state rules about points, called postulates.Example: two different points lie on exactly one line.
'Undefined' does not mean 'anything goes.' The rules limit what points can do.The rules still apply.
Theorems are then proved from the rules and the definitions.That is how the system grows.
Second check: rename the points in a drawing and every rule is still true. Add a line the rules forbid, and a rule breaks.Names don't matter; rules do.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Find the loop.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
A glossary says: a point is where lines cross.That uses 'line'.
It also says: a line is a set going through points.That uses 'point'.
Each word needs the other one first.There is no place to start.
Fix: pick starting words with no definition, and write rules about them.Undefined terms plus postulates.
Second check: draw an arrow from each word to the words it uses. Point goes to line and back to point: a loop with no start.Renaming the words does not fix a loop.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Explain why 'plane' is an undefined term. Does undefined mean we can say anything we like about a plane?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

We start with 'plane' without defining it, and we state rules about it. Undefined does not mean anything goes: the rules still limit it. Theorems are then proved from the rules.

Reveal second check

Rename things in a drawing and the rules still hold. Add a fact the rules forbid and something breaks.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
A writer says 'line is undefined, so we can assume anything handy about lines.' What's wrong? Use the rule about two points.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Undefined does not mean no rules. The rule says two different points lie on exactly one line. So we can't have two different lines through P and Q, no matter how handy it would be.

Reveal second check

A picture with two such lines breaks a stated rule, even though 'line' has no definition.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
Does every geometry book have to start with the same undefined words? Does a theorem stay true no matter what we assume?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No to both. Books can pick different starting words or rules. A theorem is true because of the rules it was proved from. Change the rules and it might not follow.

Reveal second check

A rule assumed in one book might be proved in another. Either way, every step needs a reason inside that book's system.
